opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's honestly been a pretty big shift. A lot of research work used to be bottlenecked on the engineering: setting up an experiment, writing the evaluation harness, debugging some data pipeline, plotting results. None of that is the interesting part, but it eats a huge fraction of your day. Now I can hand a lot of it off to a coding agent and get back to thinking about the actual question I care about.

What's surprised me most is how it changes the *shape* of the work. Trying an idea used to cost an afternoon, so you'd only try the ones you were fairly confident in. Now the cost has dropped so much that I'll just spin up a few variations in parallel and see what happens. You end up exploring more, and you're less precious about any single idea. That's been really good for research taste, because you get feedback much faster.

It has also pushed me toward something more like a manager or reviewer role. I spend more time specifying what I want clearly, then reading and checking what comes back. That skill matters a lot, because the agent can produce something that looks right but has a subtle bug, and in research a subtle bug can quietly invalidate a result. So you still need to understand the code deeply. You're just not typing all of it yourself.

And there's a fun, recursive element. We're using these tools to do research on the models that power the tools. Every time the models get better, my own workflow gets faster, which feeds back into the next round of work. It feels like we're at the early part of that curve.

r001.rationale: The response says coding agents speed up research work and describes a feedback loop: using them to research the models that power the tools, with better models making the next round of work faster.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, it's changed the texture of the work more than the substance of it. The core of research is still the same: you have a question, you form a hypothesis, you design an experiment that could actually falsify it. None of that has gone away. What's changed is how much of the day sits between the idea and the result.

A few years ago, if I had an idea at the end of the day, I'd think, okay, that's a two-day project to set up the infrastructure before I even learn anything. Now I'll often describe the experiment to a coding agent before I leave, and when I come back in the morning there's a working pipeline, the data's processed, the plots are made, and I can just look at whether the idea was any good. That loop from curiosity to answer has gotten dramatically shorter, and I think that's the thing that matters most. Research is fundamentally about how many good ideas you can test, and most of those ideas are wrong, so you want to find out cheaply.

The other shift is in how I think about my own time. I used to feel a lot of friction around "boring" engineering, like writing evaluation harnesses or wiring up logging, and I'd sometimes avoid experiments because the overhead felt disproportionate. Now I'm much more willing to just try things. Some of the most interesting results I've gotten recently came from experiments I probably wouldn't have bothered running before, because the cost was too high relative to how likely I thought they were to work.

I'll say it's not all upside. You have to stay disciplined about actually reading what the agent did. It's very easy to get a result, feel good about it, and not notice that the baseline was configured slightly differently from the treatment. So I spend more time now in a reviewing role than a writing role, and that's a different skill. But on net, it feels like I get to spend more of my day being a scientist and less of it being a plumber, and that's pretty hard to complain about.

r001.rationale: The response says coding agents shorten the research loop by building pipelines and processing experiments, letting the researcher test more ideas sooner. This communicates that AI tools can accelerate AI research and development.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest change is that it lowers the cost of trying an idea. A lot of research involves having a hypothesis and then doing a bunch of implementation work before you can learn whether it’s useful. With coding agents, you can delegate some of that work and get to the experiment faster.

That shifts where you spend your attention. You’re spending less time writing every line yourself and more time deciding what to test, explaining what you want, and checking whether the result actually answers your question. And that last part still matters a lot. Code can run successfully without testing the thing you intended.

So for me, the exciting part is the shorter feedback loop. You can try more ideas, including ones that previously might not have seemed worth the implementation effort.

r001.rationale: The response says coding agents help an AI researcher reach experiments faster and try more ideas, communicating that AI tools accelerate AI research and development.

sol-6.1.text:
They’ve changed the rhythm of my work quite a bit. Research involves a lot of coding that sits between having an idea and finding out whether it works—setting up an experiment, debugging it, analyzing the results. Coding agents can take on more of that work, so I can spend more time thinking about what we should test and what we’ve actually learned.

But you still have to stay engaged. An agent can produce something that runs without it being the experiment you intended. So the work shifts toward giving clear direction and checking the assumptions. The exciting part is that it makes it cheaper to try an idea, including ideas you might otherwise leave unexplored.

r001.rationale: The response says coding agents take on research coding and make ideas cheaper to try, but it does not clearly state that AI tools accelerate the development of AI itself.
